strands.title: Traces, questions and comparative reasoning
strands.focus: Bloch distinguishes deliberate from unintended testimony and origins from causes. Present observation can inform questions, without making past and present identical.

strands.title: Historical psychology and its criticisms
strands.focus: Febvre historicizes collective feelings with psychological resources and a critical Huizinga reading. Walker later questions universal claims about what people could think.

strands.title: Village reconstruction and mediated voices
strands.focus: Montaillou uses inquisitorial records for intimate social history. Such records do not provide unfiltered speech, and small scale alone does not establish Italian microstoria affiliation.

strands.title: Models and the critical turn
strands.focus: Lepetit and the editors ask how explicit models and categories can be assessed through historical evidence. Their reconsideration retains comparison and collective inquiry.
strands.works: “L’histoire et les modèles” (1988); Les Formes de l’expérience (1995)

strands.title: Observation, exceptions and generalization
strands.focus: The 1988 editorial explicitly engages microhistory; Revel’s later collective volume explores varying scale. This is an exchange, not a declaration that micro-level explanation replaces all larger patterns.

strands.title: Books as material and social productions
strands.focus: Febvre’s plan/revision and Martin’s drafting form a specific collaboration. Printing is situated among economic, technical and cultural conditions.

strands.title: Women’s history and collaborative limits
strands.focus: Duby and Perrot co-direct a multi-author project. Its Western scope and Annales’ earlier limited openings matter; feminist history has other origins and commitments.

after.scope_note: Generations overlap and disagree. The founders’ exchange programme differs from Braudel’s duration, serial economic models and the 1988–1989 methodological reconsideration. Roster contexts include named resources, critics and collaborators, not a uniform membership list. Women’s history and Italian microstoria retain independent histories; their specific exchanges do not establish a single Annales origin.

before.label: Marc Bloch
before.description: Combines comparative inquiry, social relations, belief, and critical reading of evidence. Co-founds Annales with Febvre; his work cannot be reduced to economic structures.

after.label: Marc Bloch
after.description: Comparative historian of social relations, sacred kingship and historical evidence. His Apologie distinguishes causes from beginnings and interrogates traces through questions, using present observation without collapsing historical differences.
after.scope_note: The Royal Touch and Feudal Society provide distinct historical objects; the unfinished, posthumously published Apologie (1949) addresses method. Pirenne, Maitland and Simiand appear as specific resources, not interchangeable schools. Primary methodological passages are checked; the historical books retain narrower description/metadata support and unresolved questions about generalization.

before.label: Lucien Febvre
before.description: Connects geography, belief, and historical psychology to problem-led history. Co-founds Annales; cultural questions already belong to this early project.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Problem of Unbelief in the Sixteenth Century (1942).

after.label: Lucien Febvre
after.description: Problem-led historian of geography, belief and socially organized feelings, and collaborator in book history. He challenges anachronistic ideas about Rabelais, critically adapts cultural and psychological resources, and prompts both productive reception and objections.
after.representative_figures_and_works: The Problem of Unbelief in the Sixteenth Century (1942).
after.scope_note: The Unbelief polemic (1942), sensitivity essay (1941) and Febvre–Martin book project are distinct inquiries. Historical conditions of thought should not become an unquestioned assertion that dissent was impossible. Walker’s appreciative criticism preserves that dispute. Wallon and Blondel are specific psychological resources; Martin’s substantial drafting and research are separately credited.

added.relationship: Microhistory’s changes of scale explicitly inform the 1988 critical-turn editorial
added.evidence_note: The journal’s primary statement names microhistory when reconsidering objects, observation and questions. This documents an exchange with independent work, distinct from the existing undirected Montaillou comparison.

added.relationship: Bloch explicitly credits Simiand’s account of knowledge by traces
added.evidence_note: Apologie PDF p. 34 names Simiand. The source group includes this sociological interlocutor; the arrow does not substitute Durkheim personally for Simiand or claim that all Bloch’s methods derive from sociology.

added.relationship: Febvre names Reclus’s geography among his formative readings
added.evidence_note: Combats preface explicitly recalls Géographie universelle. This is Febvre’s retrospective self-account, not evidence of formal supervision or a generic environmental determinism.

added.relationship: Burckhardt and Huizinga supply distinct resources for Febvre’s historical inquiry
added.evidence_note: Combats preface acknowledges Burckhardt; the 1941 essay works critically with Huizinga. The latter is an appreciative yet questioning reception, not adoption of every period contrast.

added.relationship: Febvre questions Huizinga’s period contrast in historical emotions
added.evidence_note: The sensitivity essay asks whether the proposed late-medieval emotional features distinguish that age from others and calls for explanation. Huizinga’s achievement is also praised; the target is a specified comparison, not all earlier cultural history.

added.relationship: Historical explanation requires questions, traces and more than an origin story
added.evidence_note: Selected Apologie passages distinguish beginnings from causes and deliberate from unintended testimony. This is a substantive methodological intervention, not evidence that Bloch founded analytic philosophy of history or directly influenced every later participant.

added.relationship: The Febvre–Martin collaboration situates printing within economic and cultural life
added.evidence_note: Publisher scope and the École des chartes account specify the 1958 book project: Martin drafts, Febvre plans and revises. This contributes a particular history of printing, not a claim that Febvre alone authored it or founded technology history.

added.relationship: Duby’s collaboration with Perrot contributes to a collective history of women
added.evidence_note: The five-volume 1991–1992 project is co-directed; Perrot’s independent feminist programme and the journal tradition’s earlier limited openings remain explicit. This names one collaboration, not the origin of women’s history or an assertion that every contributor belongs to Annales.

before.relationship: Vidal’s human geography influences Febvre and Bloch
before.evidence_note: The publisher-indexed Bloch excerpt acknowledges Vidal’s impact on historical studies; Gurevich identifies human geography as part of the Annales constellation. This classification concerns the geographical resource; the inherited reference to both founders is broader than the excerpt checked.

after.relationship: Human geography provides distinct resources for Bloch and Febvre
after.evidence_note: Bloch’s existing Vidal acknowledgment is mediated by Friedman’s indexed introduction. Febvre’s own Combats preface names Reclus as formative reading. These different examples strengthen the geographical connection without proving the identical transmission to both founders.

before.relationship: Bloch’s selective reception and Simiand’s methodological intervention connect sociology with Annales
before.evidence_note: The existing Bloch acknowledgment supports a qualified intellectual debt. Annales’ 1960 editors explicitly reprint Simiand’s 1903 essay to sustain their dialogue with social science. These are distinct reception examples, not evidence that every Annales historian follows Durkheim.

after.relationship: Bloch’s selective reception and Simiand’s methodological intervention connect sociology with Annales
after.evidence_note: The existing Bloch acknowledgment supports a qualified intellectual debt. Annales’ 1960 editors explicitly reprint Simiand’s 1903 essay to sustain their dialogue with social science. These are distinct reception examples, not evidence that every Annales historian follows Durkheim. Bloch’s Apologie explicitly credits Simiand for knowledge by traces; the checked primary passage supports this named methodological resource.

before.relationship: interdisciplinary history and the study of social structures supply methods for later social inquiry
before.evidence_note: Annales supplies interdisciplinary and structural resources for social history. These methodological contributions do not make every national new-social-history movement its descendant.

after.relationship: Interdisciplinary exchange, structures and reconsidered social categories contribute different methods
after.evidence_note: The 1929 programme, Braudel’s temporal analysis and Lepetit’s collective reconsideration of actors/practices represent different resources. These contributions do not make every national social-history movement an Annales descendant.

before.relationship: from Bloch and Febvre’s inquiry into belief to Chartier’s representations, cultural questions are developed and reworked
before.evidence_note: The history of mentalités provides a resource for cultural inquiry, with Febvre as one example. This is a bounded methodological contribution, not a claim that new cultural history simply continued mentalités or had a single origin.

after.relationship: from Bloch and Febvre’s inquiry into belief to Chartier’s representations, cultural questions are developed and reworked
after.evidence_note: Febvre’s sensitivity essay and Le Goff’s religious-history project add specified arguments to this contribution. Chartier’s representation approach reworks cultural explanation; this is not a uniform mentalités lineage or a single origin of new cultural history.

before.relationship: Montaillou invites comparison with intensive small-scale historical inquiry
before.evidence_note: Italian microstoria retains independent origins and methodological differences; Montaillou is not automatically an example of that school.

after.relationship: Montaillou invites comparison with intensive small-scale historical inquiry
after.evidence_note: The publisher describes village reconstruction through inquisitorial records. This provides a comparison of scale and evidence, not proof of Italian microstoria membership. The separate directed microhistory-to-Annales contribution concerns the 1988 editorial’s explicit methodological engagement.

before.relationship: contributes comparative social history and inquiry into collective beliefs
before.evidence_note: A specific contribution within a heterogeneous field. The individual and group links describe related levels of the same history, not independent evidence of several transmissions.

after.relationship: Co-founds Annales and contributes comparative inquiry into social relations, belief and traces
